answer:
FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, 3400–3000 BCE; co-variation, not causation):

"Between 3400 and 3000 BCE, the number of monuments (MonumentCount, social capital) and the number of axes/celts (AxesCelts, economic capital) change in locked step with each other: both rise from their window-start values (Z ≈ −0.47 and +0.37) to a synchronized peak around 3200 BCE (Z ≈ +0.91 for monuments and +2.60 for axes — the latter being the all-time maximum of the entire 4100–500 BCE series), then decline together to ≈ −0.36 and +0.80 by 3000 BCE — a strong positive co-movement (Pearson r ≈ +0.93 on the interpolated series, +0.87 on the five raw anchors). In relation to the elements of symbolic capital, the pattern is an INVERSE co-movement with the only element that actually varies in this window — house size: house size falls sharply from its all-time maximum (Z 2.05 → 0.19, Δ −1.86) while monument and axe counts rise, giving a moderate negative association (MonumentCount × HouseSize r ≈ −0.40 interpolated / −0.35 anchors; AxesCelts × HouseSize r ≈ −0.26 / −0.17). The other two symbolic-capital elements — hatchets/swords and daggers — are essentially constant across the whole window (Z ≈ −0.43 and −0.58, net change 0.00), so they show no variation and no detectable co-movement with monuments or axes. Caveats: these are Z-scores = relative deviations from the long-run mean (negative means below-average abundance, not absence); the window contains only five raw measurements per variable, so the inverse house-size relationship is fragile (leave-one-out checks can flip its sign when the extreme −3400 house-size maximum is removed), whereas the coupled Monument×Axes peak is robust (r stays +0.44 to +0.94); and the findings document co-variation, not evidence that monuments/axes respond to symbolic capital. Landscape openness declines across the window (Z +0.08 → −1.86) and tracks house size (r ≈ +0.67), providing context but not driving the hypothesis."

Overall uncertainty: MODERATE — the Monument×Axes coupling is robust and well-grounded; the inverse relationship with house size (the only quantifiable symbolic-capital element) is directionally consistent on both anchor and interpolated series but rests on only five raw points per variable, so I report it as a moderate-confidence, fragile relationship; the absence of co-movement with hatchets/swords and daggers is a data-limitation conclusion (no variation in the window), not proof of a true null.

payload.hypothesis: Between 3400 and 3000 BCE, monument count and axes/celts co-vary strongly and positively with each other (both rising to a synchronized all-time peak for axes at ~3200 BCE, then declining together), while co-varying inversely with the only symbolic-capital element that varies in the window - house size, which falls from its all-time maximum; hatchets/swords and daggers are static across the window so no co-movement is detectable for them.
payload.workflow: Loaded time_series_data.csv, capital.csv, and pollen openness CSVs; parsed European comma decimals; verified capital.csv anchors are the source of the 100-year anchor values in time_series_data.csv; extracted the 3400-3000 BCE window (CE -3400..-3000, 401 annual rows, 5 raw anchors per variable); computed net changes, peak alignment, Pearson and Spearman correlations on both the 5 raw anchors and 401-row interpolated series; ran leave-one-out fragility checks and regression slopes on anchors; used pollen/openness (MEAN PC1) as context only.
